The implication is that the Israelites were not permitted to buy and sell on the festival of **the new moon** or on **the Sabbath**, and so these merchants were impatient for those days to end. Alternate translation: [When will the new moon festival, on which we are not allowed to trade, be over, so that we may sell grain, and when will the Sabbath, on which we are also forbidden to trade, be over, so that we may open our bins of wheat]

You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to use an undersized ephah measure for grain and an oversized shekel weight for silver]

nt: As in 6:8, **the pride of Jacob** could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, since that is its meaning elsewhere, and it would make no sense to swear by something negative, such as sinful pride. Alternate translation: [by this land that Jacob’s people are so proud of] or (2) Yahweh himself. This would then be equivalent to the phrase in 6:8, “The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his soul.” Alternate translation: [by himself, of whom Jacob’s people are so proud]

Here, **Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may Yahweh punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If I ever forget…, then may Yahweh punish me severely…” But since Yahweh is speaking, stating this would not make sense. It may be clearest to translate the oath as a positive statement, as in the UST.
